_: Glabrous (ridged) skin of the palm, finger pads and sole: no hair, no sebaceous glands, a thick stratum corneum (palm ~47, heel ~86 cell layers), epidermis 0.3-0.8 mm, friction ridges ~0.4-0.55 mm pitch, dense eccrine sweat glands (palm ~240, sole ~290 /cm2) that open on the ridges. Friction depends above all on moisture: it peaks at an intermediate moisture and on smooth impermeable surfaces climbs with dwell as sweat is occluded. Stack in contact.solver: the finger pad, with palm and heel variants. SKIN lane 11-07.

loss_factor_impact.src: 2 x the impact damping ratios below (from energy_loss_fraction: e = sqrt(1 - L), zeta from e = exp(-pi zeta / sqrt(1 - zeta^2))); an equivalent single-mode value for a whole contact pulse. how a solver uses it: integrate the Prony set (deform.viscoelastic.prony) as internal variables in an implicit step (one exponential update per term per step; stable at any dt) on top of the hyperelastic stress, so a 1-10 ms slap sees the short-time stiffness and loses energy in the 1-10 ms terms; do not use Rayleigh damping fitted to the ~15 Hz wobble: beta-damping gives zeta = beta * omega / 2, so a beta set for zeta 0.15 at 15 Hz (beta 3.2 ms) gives zeta ~5 at 250-500 Hz (a 1-2 ms pulse): over-damped, the slap goes dead. Where only one number fits, use the loss factor at the pulse's frequency f ~ 1 / (2 x contact time), zeta = tan_delta / 2.

qlv._: Fung quasi-linear viscoelasticity (QLV) for the glabrous pads, 11-08 (library lane). Stress (or force) is the convolution of a reduced relaxation G(t), G(0)=1, with the rate of an instantaneous elastic response: sigma(t) = integral_0^t G(t - s) d sigma_e(eps(s))/ds ds (force form: F(t) = integral G(t - s) dF_e(x(s))/ds ds). Solver recipe: per contact point keep one state per Prony term; with G = g_inf + sum g_i exp(-t/tau_i), each step h_i <- exp(-dt/tau_i) h_i + g_i exp(-dt/(2 tau_i)) (sigma_e[n+1] - sigma_e[n]) and sigma = g_inf sigma_e + sum h_i; the Fung continuous spectrum (C, tau1, tau2) is run through its prony_equivalent (one term per decade). The loss comes only from the relaxing fraction (1 - g_inf) acting on the exponential stiffness; it is not a damping coefficient to tune. Checked here (qlv_check): with these measured sets a single load-unload of the pad loses 0.18-0.37 (finger) and 0.05-0.41 (heel), so QLV of the pad alone gives e >= ~0.77; the measured in-vivo 0.79-0.81 losses include the voluntary tap loop and the limb (qlv_check.consequence).

finger_monotonic_tap_loss.src: computed here (scratch qlv_loss.py / qlv_asym.py, imposed displacement, Ein and Eout as JINDRICH03 defines them): the Jindrich set peaks at ~0.37 loss (e ~0.79); its 81 % comes from a voluntary 80-170 ms tap with an impact transient and continued muscle-driven loading, not one elastic bounce. JINDRICH03: the pulp absorbs ~60 % of the finger's kinetic energy, the rest goes to proximal musculoskeletal elements

heel_monotonic_loss.src: computed here with LEDOUX05 G and B 9 at 40 % strain, half-sine imposed displacement

consequence.v: QLV of the pad alone bounds a free bounce at e ~0.77-0.9; the measured 0.23-0.73 band at body level needs the striking limb's own losses (finger, hand and arm soft tissue and joints; KINOSHITA93's shank tissue) in the contact, as a second QLV body or the limb's soft-tissue stack, not a larger pad damping

loss_vs_freq_measured.src: WIERT12 Table 1 (7 adults, index fingertip, tangential sinusoidal sweep 20-500 Hz, 0.5 N normal load, no slip, small amplitude, nail free): Kelvin-Voigt k and b per subject (M); tan delta = 2 pi f b / k computed here (D). 100 and 300 Hz inside the measured band; 1000 Hz is the Kelvin-Voigt fit run past 500 Hz (extrapolated). Corner (tan delta = 1) ~100 Hz: elastic below, viscous above, inertia negligible to 500 Hz. k and b scale ~ (normal force)^0.35 (Table 2), so a pad pressed harder keeps tan delta about the same. This is the whole pad as a lumped tangential load (skin + pulp + contact), not a bulk material; it agrees with Nakazawa 2000 (b 2.0 N s/m, quoted in WIERT12)
loss_vs_freq_measured.method: fingertip mechanical impedance (high-mobility voice-coil probe, closed-loop, WIERT12RSI), Kelvin-Voigt fit, tangential direction

G_storage_loss_vs_freq_measured_kPa.src: WIERT12 Table 1 effective complex Young's modulus from the contact stiffness (Cerruti, K = 8 a G / (2 - nu), nu 0.5): E and eta per subject (M), means here; E'' = 2 pi f eta and G = E / 3 computed here (D); 1000 Hz extrapolated. An effective bulk value of the pad seen through its contact (~4.5-6.5 mm contact radius), not of the skin alone (skin E is MPa-scale)

loss_vs_freq_normal_measured._: NORMAL-direction (indentation) small-amplitude loss of the index fingertip pad, 11-08 (library lane, for the contact solver). tan delta = omega b / k of the lumped spring-damper (mass excluded: it stores, it does not lose). Answer: the normal loss is of the same order as the tangential (tan delta ~1 near 100-150 Hz, ~2 at 250 Hz, rising ~ f above); both directions are viscous-dominated above ~100 Hz. The big gap is between these vibration impedances and the slow-tap QLV set (Jindrich 2003), not between directions.

best_estimate.src: KERN23 ch. 3.1.6.2/3.1.6.3 (orig. KERN08): index finger, normal excitation by a plate, 1-6 N, contactors 2-15 mm dia, 20-2000 Hz, 8 subjects, 192 sweeps: |Z| falls 20 dB/decade (elastic) up to an anti-resonance at ~100-150 Hz, then is flat ('pure damping'); 'well balanced elasticity and damping' to ~150 Hz. Taken here: corner f_c = k/(2 pi b) ~ 125 Hz (100-150), so tan delta = f / f_c. The anti-resonance read as the elastic-viscous corner is an approximation (D).

range.src: low end KERN23 f_c 150 Hz; high end the LUNDSTROM84 lumped fit below (f_c ~34 Hz). Above 500 Hz both are model extensions (KERN23 shape is measured to 2 kHz; the k-b values are not).

kern_plate_normal.src: KERN23 / KERN08 (M: corner/anti-resonance 100-150 Hz, level 10-20 dB, 20 dB/decade elastic slope, flat above; tan delta D here). Large 15 mm plate: resonance moves 150 -> 80 Hz with force; smaller contactor -> higher anti-resonance. dB reference assumed 1 N s/m (E); the parameter table is in the book's appendix, not read. 2 N excitation amplitude, sweep high to low

lundstrom_point_impedance.src: LUNDSTROM84 abstract (M: 20-10000 Hz, 6 subjects, 10 hand sites; |Z| falls to a minimum at the skin natural frequency, ~200 Hz at the distal finger, then rises ~ f) + SOFTRAT thesis review of LUNDSTROM84 (M, secondary: distal finger points ~22 N s/m at 100 Hz, 25-30 N s/m at 40 Hz, 'governed by the resistance'; contactors 0.5-1 cm2). Fit here (D): Z = b + i(omega m - k/omega) with natural freq 200 Hz through |Z|(40 Hz)=27.5 and |Z|(100 Hz)=22. Sensitive to the secondary |Z| values (indicative, upper bound); static force not retrieved

hajian_howe_whole_finger.v: whole finger about the MCP joint (2-20 N extension), second-order fit to ~20 ms transients: mass, damping, stiffness per subject; numbers not retrieved (abstract only). Not a pad property; damping ratio extension ~1.7x abduction

retardation_time_ms.src: tau_v = b / k = 1 / (2 pi f_c): KERN23 f_c 100-150 Hz -> 1.1-1.6 ms; LUNDSTROM84 fit -> 4.7 ms. For the solver: a Kelvin-Voigt dashpot b = tau_v k in parallel with the pad's elastic law gives tan delta = omega tau_v (rises ~ f), which no finite Prony set with g_inf 0.82 reproduces

compare_tangential.src: WIERT12 tan delta at 250 Hz = 0.91 x 2.5 and 0.65 x 2.5 (from loss_vs_freq_measured); JINDRICH03 from loss_factor_vs_freq

conditions_and_caveats.v: Small amplitude (um to tens of um) vibration on a pre-loaded pad (KERN 1-6 N, 2-15 mm discs; WIERT12 0.5 N flat, tangential). The lumped b includes energy carried away as waves into the finger (radiation) as well as local tissue viscosity; in a slap both leave the rebound. At mm-scale slap strains the exponential stiffness raises k; WIERT12 shows k and b scale together (~F^0.35) and KERN 4-10 dB global rise with force, so tan delta is roughly held, but large-strain normal dynamic loss at 100-500 Hz was not found measured.

loss_vs_freq_normal_measured.method: mechanical point/plate impedance (force and velocity under sinusoidal sweep), lumped spring-damper(-mass) reading, normal direction
